No retrieved evidence establishes 64 uniform negatives as optimal for GRU4Rec sampled cross-entropy. The official implementation defaults to 2,048 additional negatives and reports that roughly 500–1,000 may have little throughput impact, depending on hardware. It also buffers samples to reduce CPU sampling overhead. These results concern its optimized implementation; they do not establish the runtime of this harness’s per-position sampling. More negatives increase scoring work and intermediate storage, but end-to-end cost requires measurement. [GRU4Rec documentation](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec)

Uniform sampling does not eliminate popularity shortcuts. A sequential-recommendation study comparing sampling methods across three datasets found random sampling favored head items, while popularity-based and in-batch sampling produced more balanced performance, sometimes sacrificing aggregate accuracy. Thus, better HR@10 against uniform evaluation negatives would not alone demonstrate stronger personalization. [Prakash et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)

Unobserved items can be relevant, so sampled negatives can be false negatives. Increasing sample count increases opportunities to encounter them; the effect on learning depends on their scores and loss weights. Hard-negative sampling can be more vulnerable than uniform sampling. A defensible experiment would compare 64 with larger counts, such as 256 and 1,024, using independently trained single-model trials, fixed seeds and the pinned validation protocol; record macro HR@10 and GPU time. Exclude known training positives without consulting held-out labels. This sweep is an experimental recommendation, not an established optimum. [Revisiting Negative Sampling](https://doi.org/10.1145/3522672)
